theme: David’s last words; the mighty men; the census and plague
readingInstruction: Read 2 Samuel 23:1-24:25. These are David’s last words, the roll of his mighty men, and the story of the census and the plague. Notice how the book ends: with a sin, a sacrifice, and an altar.
settingTheScene: The last chapters of 2 Samuel are an appendix, standing outside the main story. David speaks his final oracle, and the narrator lists his mighty men. Then comes an account of David numbering the people, a sin that brings a plague on Israel. The plague stops at the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite, where David builds an altar. This is the place where the temple will rise.
observation: “The oracle of David, the son of Jesse… the sweet psalmist of Israel” (23:1).
“The Spirit of the LORD speaks by me; his word is on my tongue” (23:2).
“When one rules justly over men, ruling in the fear of God, he dawns on them like the morning light, like the sun shining forth on a cloudless morning” (23:3-4).
“For does not my house stand so with God? For he has made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and secure” (23:5).
Three mighty men break through the Philistine camp to bring David water from Bethlehem, and he pours it out to the LORD (23:13-17).
David orders Joab to number the people, and afterward his heart strikes him: “I have sinned greatly in what I have done” (24:1-10).
David says, “Let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is great; but let me not fall into the hand of man” (24:14).
“I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing” (24:24).
interpretation:
David’s last words are a reflection on kingship, and they sketch the portrait of the ideal king: one who rules justly in the fear of God. Such a king is like the morning light, like the sun after rain. The poem describes what David was meant to be and often was not. It is also an unwitting description of the coming Messiah. David says that God “has made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and secure.” At the end of his life, his hope is in the covenant, not in his own record.

The story of the three mighty men and the water from Bethlehem is a small gem. David longs for a drink from the well of his hometown. Three of his warriors risk their lives to get it. When they bring it, David will not drink. He pours it out to the LORD, saying that it is the blood of men who risked their lives. He sees their devotion as too holy to be consumed. It is a gesture of honor, and a sign that David understood the worth of sacrifice.

The census in chapter 24 is puzzling at first. Why was it a sin? The text does not say, but the likely issue is pride and self-reliance: counting the nation’s military strength as if the king’s power came from numbers. Even Joab sees the problem. David is struck in conscience and confesses. The prophet Gad offers three punishments, and David’s choice is a mark of his character: “Let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is great.” Seventy thousand die. When the angel stretches out his hand over Jerusalem, “the LORD relented.”

David’s response is to buy the threshing floor and build an altar. “I will not offer burnt offerings that cost me nothing.” True worship involves cost. The plague stops, and the site becomes the temple mount (2 Chronicles 3:1). The book that began with a barren woman at a sanctuary ends with a king at an altar. A kingdom built on sacrifice and mercy.
connection: Jesus is the “sun shining forth on a cloudless morning” of righteous rule (Malachi 4:2; Luke 1:78-79). He is the king who does not count his strength in numbers but gives himself. The place where the plague stopped became the place of sacrifice, and the greater sacrifice at Jerusalem turned away God’s wrath for good (Romans 3:25; Hebrews 9:11-14). David’s refusal to offer what costs nothing is fulfilled in Christ, who gave everything.
application:
Ask if you are tempted to measure your security by numbers: income, followers, savings, or influence.

Think about what worship costs you. Is there anything you offer God that costs you nothing?

Pour out something precious to the LORD today, in gratitude.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to keep you from trusting in numbers or success.
Thank him for an everlasting covenant secure in all things.
Thank him for the altar where wrath was turned away.
